young.html: After their long climb out of Hell, Dante and his guide Virgil come out on a beach at dawn. The stars are bright, the air is fresh, and in front of them rises an enormous mountain from the sea. This is Purgatory, the second part of Dante's great poem, the Purgatorio.

In Dante's poem, Purgatory is a place of hope. The souls here are sorry for the wrongs they did, and they climb the mountain to become good all the way through. On each of seven ledges, called terraces, they practice the opposite of one bad habit. The proud learn to be humble; the grumpy learn to be gentle. And they help each other, singing and praying as they go.

young.name: gb-dante-cosmos
young.cap: Climb the mountain from the shore to the garden at the top. Tap a level to read about it.

young.html: At the gate, an angel marks seven letters on Dante's forehead. On every terrace, an angel brushes one away, and Dante feels lighter, so climbing gets easier the higher he goes. At the very top is a beautiful garden, and there Dante meets Beatrice, the friend he loved, who will guide him the rest of the way.

Seven steps up. Draw a mountain with seven ledges. On each ledge, write one bad habit and its opposite good habit: pride and humility, envy and kindness, anger and gentleness, laziness and eagerness, greed and generosity, overeating and moderation, selfish wanting and self-control. Which good habit would you most like to practice this week? Draw yourself on that ledge.

full.html: Dante pictures Purgatory as a mountain on an island in the southern ocean, exactly opposite Jerusalem on the globe. (Ulysses glimpsed it before his ship went down.) It was formed, the poem explains, when Satan fell from heaven and the land fled from him. Dante and Virgil arrive at dawn on Easter Sunday, and the poem's mood changes at once.

full.text:
O'er better waves to speed her rapid course
The light bark of my genius lifts the sail,
Well pleas'd to leave so cruel sea behind;
And of that second region will I sing,
In which the human spirit from sinful blot
Is purg'd, and for ascent to Heaven prepares.
full.author: Dante

full.html: Unlike Hell, Purgatory has time, sunlight, music and friendship. The souls want to be here; they know their climb will end in Heaven. Prayers of the living, they say, can speed them on. This rests on the teaching of the medieval Church, which Dante shared; later, Protestant reformers rejected the idea of Purgatory. The poem presents it as Dante's faith imagined it.

full.name: gb-dante-cosmos
full.cap: From the shore to the Earthly Paradise: Ante-Purgatory, the gate, the seven terraces and the garden.

full.text: From the shore to the gate

items: The shore (Cantos I and II): the old Roman Cato guards it. Virgil washes Dante's face of the grime of Hell and ties a reed, a plant that bends without breaking, around his waist as a sign of humility. An angel steers a boat of souls across the sea, and among them is Dante's friend Casella, a musician, who sings one of Dante's own poems.
Ante-Purgatory (Cantos III to VIII): souls who put off turning to God must wait before they can begin. Dante meets old friends and talks with rulers resting in a flowered valley.
The gate (Canto IX): three steps, an angel with a sword and two keys, and seven P's, for the Latin peccatum ("sin"), traced on Dante's forehead.

full.html: On each terrace the souls are cured of one of the seven capital sins, the roots of the others in medieval teaching. They meditate on examples of the opposite virtue, often from the life of Mary, and on warnings of the vice; an angel sings one of the Beatitudes and brushes away a P. Midway up, Virgil explains why there are seven, in one of the poem's great speeches.

full.text:
"Creator, nor created being, ne'er,
My son," he thus began, "was without love,
Or natural, or the free spirit's growth. ...
Hence thou must infer
That love is germin of each virtue in ye,
And of each act no less, that merits pain."
full.author: Dante
full.note: Shortened: twelve lines are left out where the dots are.

full.html: Virgil's point: every act comes from some love. Good acts come from love rightly aimed; wrongs come from love gone astray in one of three ways. Love can be aimed at harm to others (pride, envy and anger); it can be too weak for the highest good (sloth); or it can be too strong for lesser goods (greed, gluttony, and an excessive love of bodily pleasure, called lust).

full.html: In Canto XVI, on the terrace of anger, a soul explains that the stars may stir our feelings but do not decide our choices: we have free will, and if the world goes wrong, the cause lies in us. On the terrace of greed the mountain shakes and the souls sing, because one of them, the Roman poet Statius, has finished his cleansing. He climbs on with Dante and Virgil to the top.

Before the last climb, Dante must pass through fire. He is terrified until Virgil reminds him that Beatrice waits beyond it. Then, at the top, Virgil gives his last words: Dante's will is now free, upright and whole, and he may follow it; Virgil crowns him master of himself. In the Earthly Paradise, the Garden of Eden, a great procession appears, and Beatrice comes, veiled. When Dante turns to Virgil, Virgil is gone; reason has brought him as far as it can.
Dante drinks from two rivers: Lethe, which takes away the memory of sin, and Eunoë, which restores the memory of good. The canticle ends with him made new and ready to rise to the stars.
Thinking Purgatory is a milder Hell. In the poem they are opposites. Hell's souls are fixed in what they chose; Purgatory's souls are changing, gladly, and every one of them will reach Heaven.

deep.text: A poem of friendship and art

deep.html: Purgatorio is full of artists. Dante meets musicians, painters and poets: the miniaturist Oderisi, who warns that fame passes quickly; Sordello, a poet of Virgil's own Mantua; Statius; and on the last terrace two poets Dante admired, one of whom answers him in Provençal. It is the canticle where Dante thinks hardest about his own art and its pride.

Virgil cannot enter Heaven; in the poem he lives in Limbo, among the good who lived before Christ. His leaving is one of the most moving moments in the poem, and readers still discuss what it means that the guide Dante loved most must turn back.

items: Is Virgil right that every wrong act comes from love gone astray? Try it on an example.
Can people really change their habits from the inside? What helps?
Why does climbing get easier as Dante goes higher?
What does it mean to be "master of yourself"?

deep.html: Compare Aquinas on the virtues and the passions, two rungs back, and Augustine's City of God, which defines virtue as love set in the right order.

questions: Which of the seven bad habits do you see most in the world around you? Which good habit would cure it?
In Purgatory the souls help each other. How does helping others make it easier to change?
Why does Dante put Purgatory in the open air, with sunlight and music, instead of underground?
Virgil says every good act and every wrong act comes from some kind of love. Can you think of an example?
How do you think Dante felt when Virgil disappeared? Have you ever had to say goodbye to a guide or teacher?
care: This rung presents the medieval Christian idea of Purgatory as Dante imagined it, noting that Christians have disagreed about it. Nothing in it needs special care for young readers.
